correctness.rationale: Exact analytic matrix multiplication yields mn(m-n) coefficients and the Wronskian leading band. The full finite-band counting lemma is proved by low-rank/low-norm cutoffs, blockwise Toeplitz moments, and Riemann summation. The O(k^-4) remainder has s_N=O(N^-4), handled by Weyl inequalities with a sublinear comparison index. Monomial case has a closed exact diagonal weighted shift singular spectrum, reproduced by 4815 rational tests. No finite experiment is treated as infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The independently checked claim combines a full all-polynomial commutation criterion, the explicit Wronskian leading symbol, sharp cubic singular-value constant and its Schatten boundary. The accessible motivating full-text paper proves individual-operator quasinilpotency but has no such pair-commutator classification. General Toeplitz singular-distribution literature is used as a theorem ingredient; it does not by itself identify the Volterra cancellation nor Wronskian. Specialist priority risk remains.
residual_risks: A general band-dominated pseudodifferential Weyl theorem may yield the band-counting ingredient; no novel claim is made for that general theorem.
A specialist historical result could already contain the exact Volterra-pair Wronskian formula; mathematical searching cannot certify universal priority.
Paywalled Chapter 9 and linked published result summaries were not read in full; neither was used to assert full-document noncoverage.

value.rationale: The problem is natural for noncommuting pairs of analytic Volterra integration operators. The theorem gives a complete polynomial-class commutativity boundary and sharp new singular decay and all-Schatten classification. The Wronskian gives a structural, calculable invariant for cancellation, not a decorative numerical special case; it distinguishes commuting proportional derivatives from infinite-rank cubic smoothing. The result has implications for approximation and trace ideal behavior. It does not claim a general nonpolynomial theorem.
